title: The Input Dilemma
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Using her own habit of keeping dozens of browser tabs open, Melissa Muth Martinez examines the CliftonStrengths Input theme, the drive to collect and archive information. She credits it as a real gift for research and connecting ideas across domains, and notes that high-Input people ask better questions and are hard to blindside. She then names the trap: gathering can substitute for doing, delaying decisions under a reasonable-sounding need for one more piece of context, and the collection can become a second job. Her remedy is a set of six questions to test whether one has enough to act, framing Input as fuel to be used with discipline. The practical takeaway is knowing when to close the tabs and move to action.
points: The Input strength is a genuine asset for research and cross-domain connection, but gathering can become a way of delaying decisions.
The curation trap occurs when a personal archive consumes more bandwidth than it returns and becomes a second job.
Six questions, such as what decision the input supports, what would change with more information and what waiting costs, help decide when enough is enough.
Asking whether one collects because it is useful or because it is comfortable separates strategy from habit.
quotes: Broadly speaking, the challenge with Input is that the act of gathering can get in the way of doing. More specifically, it can become a way of delaying decision or action under an entirely reasonable-sounding justification that we just need a little more information before we can move forward.

If you’ve ever found yourself re-reading something you’ve already processed because you want to make sure you haven’t missed anything, you know exactly what I’m describing. The system that is supposed to support our thinking becomes more like a second job.
This is genuinely a gift. In the context knowledge work especially, the ability to hold a lot of information and make unexpected connections across domains is enormously valuable.
What I’ve started to believe is that Input is less a goal than it is fuel. But we need to use that fuel responsibly.

I share these questions not to shame Input—I, for one, have seen the incredible value behind it. But they are meant to add a small layer of intentionality to a behavior that, for high-Input people, typically runs on autopilot.

Less can indeed be more, depending on the context, of course, but the goal is really isn’t to collect less. What we need to do is be disciplined in knowing why we’re collecting, and to recognize the moment when the most useful thing we can do is stop and use what we already have.
